newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian canola output seen up, prices to fall.
newsitem.headline: Australian canola output seen up, prices to fall.

text.p: Australian canola production is seen rising 32 percent in 1997/98 (July-June), but prices are expected to fall in the year ahead, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said on Tuesday.
ABARE, the Australian government's main commodities forecasting agency, said world oilseed prices were expected to fall in 1997/98 on expanded output and higher stocks.

ABARE said in its June quarter Australian Commodities report that it expected Australia to produce about 2.035 million tonnes of oilseeds in 1997/98, up 12.7 percent from estimated output of 1.805 million tonnes in 1996/97.
Australian canola production was expected to rise to 813,000 tonnes from an expected 616,000 tonnes in 1996/97 with an increase in the area used for planting, ABARE said.

But the latest quarterly forecast was down on the March quarter estimate of 822,000 due to the dry start to the season in eastern Australia, which was partially offset by a near ideal start in Western Australia.
Australia produced 1.403 million tonnes of oilseeds in 1995/96, including 561,000 tonnes of canola.
Australia's domestic use of canola was forecast to increase by 20 percent to 265,000 tonnes in 1997/98 as a result of further expansion in processing capacity, the bureau said.
"With this increase in capacity, canola oil supplies are forecast to exceed domestic requirements for the third consecutive year," ABARE said.
It said canola oil exports are forecast to be nearly 20,000 tonnes, about double the amount shipped in 1996/97.
"Oilseed meal prices are also forecast to fall in 1997/98 as a result of increased supplies (particularly soymeal) and lower import demand," ABARE said.
The bureau said in contrast prices for vegetable oils are forecast to increase in 1997/98 as rising consumer demand results in stocks remaining tight.
World oilseeds production was forecast to increase by four percent in 1997/98 from an expansion in area sown to soybeans, canola and sunflowers.
Most of the increase in soybean plantings was forecast to occur mainly in the United States, it said.
World consumption of oilseeds is forecast to rise by nearly three percent in 1997/98 as a result of further increases in world oilseeds processing for both meal and oil, ABARE said.
"Economic and population growth is expected to result in greater demand for both livestock products and vegetable oils, particularly in Asia," the bureau said.
